title: After Finishing Clinical Clerkships at Tulane University School of Medicine and The Chinese University of Hong Kong
paragraphs: I took part in four weeks of hospital clerkships at Tulane University in Louisiana, USA, and four weeks at The Chinese University of Hong Kong in Hong Kong. My clerkship at Tulane University was originally planned for three months, but it was shortened to one month because of the host's circumstances, and thanks to the efforts of the professors of the International Collaboration Office, I was suddenly able to do a clerkship in Hong Kong as well. I was full of anxiety at first, but as a result I was able to experience both Asian and American medicine, and it was a very rich and irreplaceable experience.

[Life at Tulane University] Tulane University is a base hospital in the southern United States, located in New Orleans, the birthplace of jazz. (According to a travel guidebook, it is also said to be the Harvard of the South?) New Orleans has a unique culture that mixes Black culture and French culture, the Creole food is delicious, and the townscape is stylish like a theme park; it was a truly wonderful city. In my clerkship, I rotated for two weeks each through cardiology and endocrinology. In cardiology I was assigned to the CCU team. I had no access to charts, there were no other students, and the doctors were all busy with their own work, so at first I could barely grasp the patients' conditions while joining the rounds. But by actively asking questions about patients and talking about treatment in Japan, I think the distance between me and the doctors gradually narrowed. By the way, during this rotation I got shingles, but through a resident I had become friends with, I was seen by a dermatology attending without waiting, was prescribed valacyclovir, and it was settled without trouble. (Even so, the first-visit fee was 20,000 yen and the medicine cost 30,000 yen.) I experienced firsthand the high cost of American healthcare and the poor access to it, which gave me a chance to think about the insurance system. The endocrinology clerkship was centred on outpatient clinics. The range of diseases was broader than in the CCU, and there were many cases rarely seen in Japan, such as a girl with undiagnosed virilization for ten years, a diabetic patient with a BMI over 60, and a patient with tetany from hypocalcemia caused by a misunderstanding of the dose of medicine after parathyroidectomy, and it was very interesting. Perhaps as a result of approaching proactively, at UMC (a public hospital) I was allowed to do the first touch, order tests and think about diagnosis and treatment with the doctors, and I had a fulfilling clerkship. In endocrinology everyone was relaxed and got along well, and the attending taught me about image reading and interesting cases in his spare time, so it was educational and every day was very enjoyable. On the last day, the fellow in charge bought a cake and celebrated with me and said it had been fun working together, and I was truly happy because I felt my efforts had been recognised.

[Life at The Chinese University of Hong Kong] At The Chinese University of Hong Kong, I rotated for four weeks through cardiothoracic surgery. In contrast to America, from the first day they were very welcoming and educational toward international students, so much so that at first I was rather bewildered. The patients' official language is Cantonese, but in the outpatient clinic and on the ward the students translated what the patients said into English and let me do the physical examination together, the doctors explained during surgery, and every day after surgery they gave a mini-lecture, so from morning to night it was very fulfilling. More than 700 operations a year are performed in cardiac surgery and thoracic surgery combined, and in one month I could observe almost the full range of surgeries, from CABG, valve replacement and repair, thoracic aortic replacement, lung cancer surgery and bullectomy to thymoma resection and pleurodesis. What impressed me during the clerkship was how diligent the students were. Although Hong Kong has about the same population as Aichi Prefecture, it has only two medical schools, so the students are all truly excellent. Medical students generally do not do club activities or part-time jobs, and as I was also lacking in knowledge compared with the fifth-year student I did the clerkship with, I studied desperately while competing with them. In Hong Kong all higher education is conducted in English, and the medical staff and students are very fluent in English. However, there were also many difficulties: the strong Cantonese accents often made it hard to tell whether it was Cantonese or English, or to hear them, and since they use British English, the conventional units of blood glucose and creatinine are different. But everyone was fond of Japan, greeting me with "konnichiwa" in Japanese in the operating room and telling me memories of their trips to Japan, so there was never a shortage of topics, and I spent every day very comfortably. In daily life, besides sightseeing and extracurricular activities, sharing meals and sleep with 小山さん in a tiny two-person room of about five tatami mats is a very good memory. I was very happy to have made a friend with whom I could share happy things and cheer each other up when we were down, and I am truly grateful to 小山さん.

[After finishing clerkships in two countries] Through clerkships in the two countries, America and Hong Kong, I felt the various differences and the merits and demerits of both firsthand, and my horizons widened a great deal. In America I learned the importance of not giving up and engaging actively in the clerkship, and I felt the difficulty of choosing the best treatment amid many races and limited insurance coverage. In Hong Kong I learned how to build trust with patients who do not share a language, and, as a fellow Asian, I wanted to follow the students' awareness and high English ability. Throughout the whole study abroad I also learned anew how high the level of Japanese healthcare is, which was a very good opportunity to reconsider my own country's healthcare system and, further, its culture and national character, and I think that overcoming various difficulties made me grow to no small degree. I sincerely thank Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and everyone in the International Collaboration Office who gave me this valuable opportunity, 西尾さん, the professors of the Frontier-kai, the professors of Tulane University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, and my family, friends and everyone who supported me.
